q-341253.name: Question 1
q-341253.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,\pi ),$ the even extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,\pi ), \\ F(-x), & x\in (-\pi ,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-\pi ,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =F(-x) \\  & =(-x){e}^{-x} \\  & =-x{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-2) & =-(-2){e}^{-(-2)}=2{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-341240.html:
Question 5
?

Let F(x)=x3−x for x∈[0,π), and let f(x) be the even extension of F(x) to x∈(−π,π). What is f(x) for x∈(−π,0)?

a
−x3+x
b
x3−x
c
|−x3+x|
d
|x|3+|x|
e
−x3−x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If F(x) is defined on x∈[0,π), the even extension of F is the function f such that f(x)={F(x),x∈[0,π),F(−x),x∈(−π,0).

In this case, for x∈(−π,0), we get f(x)=F(−x)=(−x)3−(−x)=−x3+x.
q-341240.knowledge_point: Understanding the Even Extension of a Function

q-340814.name: Question 6
q-340814.problem:
$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=3{x}^{2}+2$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{0}.$

${a}_{0}=$ {{field-1}}
q-340814.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the constant term is given by

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=3{x}^{2}+2$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(3{x}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{[{x}^{3}+2x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }({\pi }^{3}+2\pi )-0 \\  & =2({\pi }^{2}+2).\end{aligned}
$$

q-340812.name: Question 11
q-340812.problem:
Let $F(x)=2x+3$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼(3+\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$
q-340812.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=2x+3$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2x+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x+3\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(2x+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{2}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((2\pi +3)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{2}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0+\frac{2}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{4(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-1)}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{4((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x)∼(3+\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

q-341257.name: Question 12
q-341257.problem:
$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=-4x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{n}.$$\,{a}_{n}=$ {{field-1}}
for $n\ge 1$
q-341257.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-4x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=-\frac{8}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{8}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{8}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{8}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{8}{n\pi }(0+\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{8(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ))}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{8(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

q-341272.name: Question 13
q-341272.problem:
Let $F(x)=7x-4$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼(-4+\frac{7\pi }{2})+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$
q-341272.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=7x-4$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(7x-4)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=7x-4\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=7 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(7x-4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{7}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((7\pi -4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{7}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0+\frac{7}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{14(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-1)}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{14((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x)∼(-4+\frac{7\pi }{2})+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{14((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

q-341270.problem:
Let $F(x)=4x-1$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼(-1+2\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$
q-341270.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=4x-1$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(4x-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=4x-1\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=4 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(4x-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{4}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((4\pi -1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{4}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0+\frac{4}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{8(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-1)}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{8((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x)∼(-1+2\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

q-341260.name: Question 15
q-341260.problem:
$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=-8x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{n}.$$\,{a}_{n}=$ {{field-1}}
for $n\ge 1$
q-341260.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-8x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=-\frac{16}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{16}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{16}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{16}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{16}{n\pi }(0+\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{16(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ))}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{16(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

f(x)∼a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nx) Let F(x)=−8x for x∈[0,π). The Fourier cosine series of the even 2π-periodic extension f(x) of F(x) is shown above. Find the expression for an.an=
16(1−(−1)n)πn2
16(1−(−1)n)πn2
4(1−(−1)n)πn2
16(1+(−1)n)πn2
16(1−(−1)n)πn
8(1−(−1)n)πn2
for n≥1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by an=2π∫0πf(x)cos⁡(nx)dx.

In our case, f(x)=−8x for x∈(0,π). So, substituting into the formula, we get an=−16π∫0πxcos⁡(nx)dx.

We use the integration by parts: u=x⇒u′=1v′=cos⁡(nx)⇒v=1nsin⁡(nx)

Thus, we obtain an=−16π(uv|0π−∫0πvu′dx)=−16π(1n[xsin⁡(nx)]0π−1n∫0πsin⁡(nx)dx)=−16nπ((π⋅sin⁡(nπ)−0⋅sin⁡(0))+1n[cos⁡(nx)]0π)=−16nπ(0+1n(cos⁡(nπ)−cos⁡(0)))=16(1−cos⁡(nπ))n2π.

Finally, since cos⁡(nπ)=(−1)n, we have an=16(1−(−1)n)πn2.
